title: Abbott to Spin Off Nutrition Unit, Cuts 2026 Sales Growth Outlook
excerpt: Abbott will carve its $8.5 billion Nutrition business, home to Similac and Ensure, into a standalone public company by end-2027, as it lowers its 2026 sales growth forecast to about 6%.
body:
• Abbott Laboratories will separate its Nutrition business, home to Similac and Ensure, into an independent publicly traded company by the end of 2027.
  • The unit has about 16,000 employees, 14 production sites and roughly $8.5 billion in annual sales; shareholders will receive shares in the new company in a tax-free distribution.
  • Abbott cut its 2026 sales growth forecast to about 6% from 6.5% to 7.5%, while third-quarter revenue was $13.01 billion and adjusted earnings were $1.42 per share, in line with estimates.
  • For investors, the split leaves Abbott focused on medical devices, diagnostics and established medicines, with the nutrition company to be led by Daniel Salvadori.

Abbott Laboratories said on Wednesday it will separate its Nutrition business into an independent, publicly traded company, shedding a unit that has faced a government contract loss, higher costs and litigation over its baby formula products. The company announced the plan ahead of its third-quarter results and said the separation is expected to be completed by the end of 2027, subject to customary closing conditions including regulatory approvals, according to Seeking Alpha via TradingView.

Abbott will distribute shares of the new company to its existing shareholders as a tax-free transaction. Once the separation is complete, shareholders will own shares in both listed firms.

"This separation will benefit both companies, setting each one up for maximum success in its respective market."

— Robert Ford, Chief Executive Officer, Abbott Laboratories

What Is Being Spun Off

The Nutrition business owns Similac infant formula and other well-known brands including Ensure, PediaSure and Glucerna. It has roughly 16,000 employees and 14 production sites globally and generates approximately $8.5 billion in annual sales. Reuters, in its report carried by 965 WTOU, put the unit’s sales at more than $8 billion last year.

Daniel Salvadori, Abbott’s executive vice president and group president of its Established Pharmaceuticals and Nutritional Products unit, will become chief executive of the new company. Abbott said the planned transaction will not change the 2027 outlook it plans to provide in January.

Earnings and a Lower Sales Forecast

The spin-off news arrived with a reduced outlook. Abbott now expects 2026 sales growth of about 6%, down from its prior expectation of 6.5% to 7.5%. It tightened its full-year adjusted profit per share forecast to $5.50 to $5.55, from $5.45 to $5.60.

For the third quarter, Abbott reported adjusted profit of $1.42 per share, in line with analysts’ average estimate, according to data compiled by LSEG. Total revenue was $13.01 billion, compared with an average estimate of $13 billion. In medical devices, third-quarter sales grew 6.9% to $5.83 billion, missing the $5.88 billion average estimate, hurt by weaker-than-expected sales for its heart devices.

Shares fell about 3.4% in premarket trading and were down about 4% in morning trading. J.P.Morgan analyst Robbie Marcus said the slip likely reflected the potential for nutrition value creation partially offsetting moderated underlying business fundamentals.

Why Nutrition Has Struggled

The pediatric nutrition business has been hurt in previous quarters by the loss of a major US government supply contract last year and by rising manufacturing costs for consumer packaged goods. Higher costs forced the company to raise prices, in turn suppressing demand from consumers on tight budgets.

The baby formula business has faced setbacks since a 2022 recall and the shutdown of Abbott’s Sturgis, Michigan plant, which exacerbated a nationwide shortage. The company has also faced lawsuits alleging its specialized formula for premature infants caused a potentially fatal bowel disease, and costly litigation over its baby formula products was cited by Reuters as part of the backdrop to the separation. Chief Executive Robert Ford, speaking on a post-earnings call, said outstanding legal disputes were unlikely to delay the separation and pointed to differentiated, high-growth segments within nutrition over the next decade.

A Familiar Playbook in Healthcare

Abbott joins peers including Johnson & Johnson and Medtronic that have also announced business separations in recent years, as large healthcare companies reshape portfolios to sharpen focus on higher-growth segments. After the split, Abbott’s core portfolio will be medical devices, diagnostics and established medicines — businesses Ford said have compelling growth opportunities.

What Happens Next

Investors will watch for the formal filing and capital structure of the new nutrition company, its dividend and debt plans, and any update on the formula litigation before the end-2027 completion target. For Abbott itself, the next test is execution in medical devices, where the third-quarter miss and the lower 2026 sales growth view — a trajectory RBC Capital Markets analyst Au Kendall flagged as unfavourable for 2027 — set the questions management must answer in coming quarters.
